list.listitem: Identification of poison, route of administration, and identifying amount of exposure is critical. C
General diagnostic testing such as lab work, imaging, or ECG should be guided by patient's severity and constellation of symptoms. C
Low levels of serum and erythrocyte acetylcholinesterase (AChE) support the diagnosis. C
Decontaminate the patient. C
Atropine is the mainstay of treatment. A
There is insufficient evidence to support routine use of pralidoxime in the management of acute organophosphate pesticide poisoning. B
In the US, pesticides are the most common cause of poisoning and disproportionately affect children.
Ninety-nine percent of all deaths from pesticide poisoning occur in developing countries.

Organophosphates are the basis of many pesticides, solvents, and nerve gases. They are found in insecticides commonly used in the house and garden and for flea prevention in dogs (but not cats). A list of common organophosphates are listed in .

While they are chemically diverse, the primary mechanism of organophosphates primary mechanism is to deactivate AChE, resulting in increased cholinergic (muscarinic and nicotinic) responses, primarily in smooth muscle but also in the CNS.
Some compounds have a direct effect on the inhibition of AChE, while others are converted in the liver to metabolites that inhibit AChE.
Allethrin, permethrin, piperonyl butoxide, pyrethrins, pyrethroids, N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide, and pyrethrum are not organophosphates.

Obtain history and objective proof, if possible, of the ingested product and the quantity. The diagnosis of organophosphate poisoning is based on the history of exposure and the presence of symptoms outlined in .

A common mnemonic outlining typical signs and symptoms is SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal symptoms, emesis (see ). These symptoms occur less often in children.

The constellation and severity of symptoms will depend on the type of pesticide and its toxicity, the amount involved in exposure, the route of exposure (inhalation is fastest, followed by ingestion, then dermal), and the duration of exposure (single massive exposure or chronic sublethal exposure).
Monitor for cholinergic symptoms, most notably hypoxemia and respiratory distress.

Acute exposure: Symptoms are because of continued depolarization at neuromuscular junction. Most symptoms appear within 12 to 24 hours after exposure. Respiratory failure is the most life-threatening symptom. Hypoxemia, electrolyte derangement, and acidosis are major risk factors for cardiac complications.

Intermediate syndrome: In some instances after the initial organophosphate exposure, a delayed syndrome occurs after 24 to 96 hours of exposure or apparent recovery. The symptoms include acute paralysis involving mainly proximal limb muscles, muscles of the face and neck, and respiratory muscles, which can lead to respiratory failure. The mechanism of this intermediate syndrome is not known but is thought to be separate from the acute syndrome. The intermediate syndrome is not related to the cholinergic effect of organophosphate compounds.

Organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy: Persistent peripheral nervous system impairment has been reported in patients more than two years following severe organophosphate poisoning. Motor impairment is the most marked effect, but sensory deficits have also been demonstrated. This syndrome involves progressive distal weakness and ataxia in the lower limbs, and may ultimately lead to paralysis.

Chronic organophosphate-induced neuropsychiatric disorder: Long-term exposure to low levels of organophosphates produces neuropsychiatric symptoms, including motor deficits, psychiatric disturbances, and extrapyramidal symptoms.
Organophosphates are a diverse class of chemical compounds and their symptoms vary. History is the most important guide in determining exposure and appropriate management.

Low levels of serum AChE and erythrocyte AChE (EAChE) can be used as diagnostic aids in organophosphate poisoning. Coma, respiratory failure, hemodynamic disturbances, and death are associated with a decrease of EAChE.
Glasgow coma scale, Apache II, Apache III, and SAPS scoring have been used to assess risk in acute poisoning.
ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation): The patient may require intubation to protect the airway in severe poisoning.

All clothing should be removed and bagged as hazardous materials. The patient should be washed thoroughly with soap and water. It is during this skin decontamination that healthcare workers are in the most danger of exposure.
In the case of ingestion, GI decontamination is not recommended. Many patients will be vomiting profusely and will not require further GI decontamination.
Treat any vomitus as hazardous.
Do not give ipecac or activated charcoal without recommendation from a poison center or emergency department.
Irrigate eyes if there is any ocular exposure.
Consult poison control center personnel (1-800-222-1222) for information regarding the specific agent, the length of inpatient treatment, and the duration of likely toxicity.
Anticholinergic treatment with atropine is the mainstay of treatment. Atropine is recommended immediately by the American Heart Association for severe poisoning.
Glycopyrrolate may be substituted for atropine.
Cardiac complications and electrocardiographic manifestations may occur in as many as 62% of patients. Treat any cardiac abnormalities, including prolonged Q-Tc intervals.
Treat seizures with benzodiazepines.
There is some evidence that magnesium may be of benefit. B
There is insufficient evidence to recommend pralidoxime for management of acute organophosphate poisoning. B However, the American Heart Association states use is "reasonable."
There is insufficient evidence to support routine use of plasma or urinary alkalinization. B
Intermediate syndrome: The symptoms do not respond well to atropine or pralidoxime; treatment is mainly supportive.
Read and follow label instructions and safety warnings.
Use gloves and other protective clothing when using or applying pesticides.
Wash hands after using pesticides.
Ensure proper ventilation when applying pesticides indoors, eg, on pets.
Do not transfer pesticides to other containers that children may mistake for food.
Keep pesticides and poisons stored out of reach of children.

The prognosis for most patients treated early is excellent; most patients fully recover in 7 to 10 days. In developing countries, medical management is difficult, with case fatality generally more than 15%.
Acute and long-term exposures have been shown to increase risk of Parkinson's disease, leukemia, and suicidality.
For patients who have mild poisoning, no follow-up outpatient treatment is needed.
Intermediate syndrome has been known to persist for 4 to 18 days; recovery from intermediate syndrome can take up to 12 months.

Marked decrease in EAChE is associated with poor prognosis in patients with acute organophosphate poisoning. This finding can be used as a guide for more intensive medical management such as mechanical ventilation.
Children born to mothers with chronic insecticide exposure have impaired fetal growth. They have lower weight and length at birth.
Typically described clinical syndromes in adults often do not occur in children.

In pediatric poisoning cases, medication doses similar to those administered in adults can be used. This is a safe and effective alternative to weight- and age-based dosing, which can be inaccurate in emergency situations.

feature.caption: Treatment of Acute Organophosphate Poisoning.
feature.feature_body:
Atropine Sulfate Magnesium Sulfate
Dosage and administration 1-2 mg repeated every 10 minutes until clearing of secretions. Give IV, IM, via endotracheal tube, or nebulized. May go up to 300 mg/day 4 g/day
Mechanism Anticholinergic. does not reverse the effects of the organophosphate on AChE Inhibition of acetylcholine and organophosphate antagonism
Clinical notes Tachycardia and dilated pupils are not contraindications to stopping administration Magnesium, when added to atropine, will decrease hospitalization days and mortality rate in patients with organophosphate poisoning
Data from Pajoumand A, Shadnia S, Rezaie A, Abdi M, Abdollahi M. Benefits of magnesium sulfate in the management of acute human poisoning by organophosphorus insecticides. Hum Exp Toxicol 2004;23:565–569.
